PAPER: JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH Vanwinkelen et al Review Digital Interventions Targeting Healthy and Sustainable Eating Behavior: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Käbi Vanwinkelen, MA; Bram Spruyt, MA; Tim Smits, Prof Dr Media, Information and Persuasion Lab, Department of Communication Science, KU Leuven, Leuven, Belgium Corresponding Author: Käbi Vanwinkelen, MA Media, Information and Persuasion Lab, Department of Communication Science KU Leuven Parkstraat 45 Leuven 3000 Belgium Phone: 32 016326735 Email: kabi.vanwinkelen@kuleuven.be Abstract Background: Current food consumption patterns contribute to the rising prevalence of obesity and noncommunicable diseases and exacerbate environmental degradation. Digital media offer promising opportunities to promote healthier and more sustainable eating; yet, evidence regarding their effectiveness remains fragmented. Objective: The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis is (1) to evaluate the effectiveness of digital interventions in improving healthy and sustainable food consumption and (2) to identify which participant and intervention characteristics are associated with greater effectiveness. Methods: A systematic search was conducted in January 2024 and repeated in September 2025 across Web of Science, Embase, and Scopus, supplemented with forward and backward reference searching. Eligible studies were those with a quasi-experimental or longitudinal design evaluating digital interventions targeting nonclinical populations, with the aim of increasing plant-based food consumption or reducing animal-based food intake. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool. Included interventions were coded for behavior change techniques using the Behavior Change Taxonomy version 1. A random-effects meta-analysis with robust variance estimation was performed, and moderator analyses were conducted with participant and intervention characteristics. Results: Eligibility screening led to the inclusion of 52 papers published between 2004 and 2025, with 24,652 participants in total. The meta-analysis revealed a small but statistically significant positive effect of digital interventions on food consump- tion outcomes (d=0.33, 95% CI 0.25‐0.42; P<.001). However, substantial heterogeneity (I2=86%, 95% prediction interval −0.21 to 0.87) indicates considerable variation in effectiveness across intervention characteristics. A moderator analysis showed no significant difference in effectiveness (P=.53) between interventions aimed at reducing meat consumption (d=0.38, 95% CI 0.20‐0.57; P<.001) and those promoting plant-based eating (d=0.33, 95% CI 0.23‐0.42; P<.001). Although digital interventions had the strongest effects among young adults (d=0.46, 95% CI 0.30‐0.61; P<.001), age-related differences were not statistically significant. Intervention effectiveness differed significantly by platform (P=.03), with social media interven- tions (d=0.65, 95% CI 0.41‐0.90; P<.001) yielding stronger effects than other modalities. Incorporating prompts or cues significantly enhanced effectiveness (d=0.58 vs d=0.30; P=.04). Although not statistically significant, interventions including social support or behavioral comparison (both d=0.39; P<.001) yielded larger effects. Few studies included adolescents or individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds. Conclusions: This review underscores the innovative potential of digital interventions in improving eating behavior, highlighting how effectiveness varies by intervention design. Social media emerge as particularly promising, likely due to their unique social and interactive features. By pinpointing the contexts and types of digital interventions that most effectively promote plant-based eating, this study provides timely guidance for researchers and practitioners in increasingly digitalized food environments. Nonetheless, more high-quality studies are needed to confirm these insights and address the critical gap among adolescents and low socioeconomic groups. JSON: Name: socialmedia_bct_effects Title: Randomized controlled trial comparing digital delivery platforms and behavior change technique components to increase plant-based food consumption among adolescents and low-socioeconomic-status young adults Short Hypothesis: A social-media-delivered intervention incorporating prompts/cues and active social support causes a greater increase in individual daily plant-based food consumption than SMS- delivered and mobile-app-delivered interventions that lack one or both components over a 12-week intervention period. Related Work: Existing work shows small-to-moderate average effects of digital interventions on healthy and sustainable eating but substantial heterogeneity by platform, age group, and intervention content. Prior meta-analyses and systematic reviews report stronger numerical effects for social media and interventions including prompts/cues and social-support elements, while many studies rely on websites/apps, use self-reported outcomes, and underrepresent adolescents and low-SES participants. Current limitations include: (1) scarcity of randomized comparisons across delivery platforms in the same trial; (2) unclear causal contribution of specific BCT clusters (eg, prompts/cues, social support, normative messaging) due to co-occurrence and inconsistent reporting; (3) reliance on self-reported intake and short follow-up windows; and (4) inadequate sampling of adolescents and low-SES groups, limiting external validity and subgroup inference. Abstract: Problem: Digital interventions show heterogeneous effects on increasing plant-based food consumption; evidence is limited for adolescents and low-socioeconomic-status (SES) young adults and for the causal contribution of specific behavior change technique (BCT) components. Approach: Conduct a multi-arm randomized controlled trial that compares three delivery platforms (social media, SMS, mobile app) and orthogonally manipulates two BCT components (prompts/cues; active social support) to estimate platform and BCT causal effects on plant-based intake. Main contribution: Provide randomized, objective, and self-reported estimates of platform-by-BCT interactions on dietary change in adolescents and low-SES young adults, with a pre-registered analysis plan and mediation analysis to identify mechanisms. Expected outcome: Quantify whether social-media delivery combined with prompts and social support yields larger increases in plant-based consumption, and produce estimates of effect size and variability useful for practical implementation and equity-focused deployment. Experiments: Design: Multi-arm, parallel-group randomized controlled trial with 7 arms: (1) social media + prompts + social support; (2) social media + prompts only; (3) SMS + prompts + social support; (4) SMS + prompts only; (5) mobile app + prompts + social support; (6) mobile app + prompts only; (7) passive control (no intervention). Randomization: 1:1:1:1:1:1:1 stratified by age group (adolescent 13-17, young adult 18-30) and SES (low vs non-low) with block randomization. Sample size: 200 participants per arm (total N=1400). Minimum subgroup targets: ≥200 adolescents and ≥400 low-SES participants across arms. Intervention period: 12 weeks; follow-up at 3 and 6 months post-intervention. Recruitment datasets: school-based sampling frames (adolescents), community outreach and online panels targeting low-SES households, university student lists (young adults). Objective outcome subset: obtain grocery loyalty-card purchase data or digital receipts for a preconsented subset of n=600 (balanced across arms) for objective intake estimates. Primary outcome: change from baseline to 12 weeks in mean daily plant-based servings (grams/day and servings/day) measured by 3 repeated 24-hour dietary recalls averaged and corroborated by loyalty-card-derived plant-based purchase proportion. Secondary outcomes: change in red/processed meat intake (g/day), EAT-Lancet diet adherence index, ecological momentary assessment (EMA) of eating episodes, engagement metrics (impressions, replies, clicks), retention. Baselines: passive control (arm 7) and standard SMS-based informational messaging (arm 3 or 4 depending on factorial cell) as active comparator. Ablation/Factorial comparisons: between arms with vs without social support; between arms with vs without prompts to test main effects and interaction effects; pairwise platform comparisons (social media vs SMS, social media vs app, SMS vs app). Evaluation metrics and analysis: intention-to-treat mixed-effects linear regression for continuous outcomes (random intercepts for participant, fixed effects for arm, time, arm×time, baseline covariates), robust variance estimation for clustered observations, calculation of Cohen's d for pairwise contrasts, pre-specified subgroup analyses by age and SES using interaction terms, mediation analysis to test whether changes in perceived descriptive norms and social support mediate intake changes, multiple imputation for missing data, sensitivity analyses restricted to objective-outcome subset and per-protocol population. Statistical thresholds: two-sided alpha=0.05, adjust for multiple primary pairwise contrasts using family-wise error control (Holm method). Risk Factors and Limitations: Risk of contamination between arms (cross-exposure on public social media channels) that biases platform contrasts; differential attrition across arms producing informative missingness and reduced effective sample size; limited availability or completeness of loyalty-card or digital receipt data leading to biased objective estimates; self-selection bias in recruitment (participants willing to join digital trials may differ systematically in baseline motivation); measurement error in dietary recalls and EMA; platform algorithm changes or policy restrictions during the intervention period that alter exposure or engagement; insufficient representation of some demographic subgroups despite stratified targets, limiting power for moderation tests; generalizability restricted to the cultural and food-environment contexts sampled; scalability constraints if intervention relies on human-moderated social support (compute and staff requirements); potential small effect sizes requiring large samples to detect platform-by-BCT interactions.
